notes: The bars are actually gone this time — verified against your own covers rather than invented ones. Detection is rebuilt around one idea: padding is what has nothing but padding outside it. The scan now walks outward-in and stops at the first depth where three things hold at once — both edges are real seams, they sit at the same depth, and what lies outside is markedly quieter than what lies inside. That last test is what was missing: padding is a flat colour or a blur, artwork is not, and without it a bold line drawn symmetrically inside a picture could win and slice a character in half. The strength threshold is also read from the outermost slices only; measured across the whole trimmable band it picked up artwork, rose to six times its proper value, and rejected genuine borders. On a sample of sixteen covers taken from across the library, fourteen come out square to within 5%, and the two that are real 16:9 illustrations are left untouched. Padding made of a blurred enlargement of the cover is now detected too. The previous pass looked for uniform bands, which finds black or solid-colour bars but is defeated by the far more common case: the square sleeve sitting on a blurred, stretched copy of itself. A blur is a smooth gradient, so no column is ever uniform and the scan stopped on its first pixel. What actually separates that padding from the artwork is not flatness but detail — a blur has almost no structure between neighbouring columns, while the edge of the inset art is a hard seam. The scan now measures that difference and looks for the seam, requiring one on both sides at roughly the same depth, since padding added to centre an image is symmetric and an off-centre photograph is not. A picture that merely has a quiet edge is left alone. The bars beside the artwork are gone. They were never a border the app drew — they are pixels inside the cover itself: a square sleeve padded out to 16:9 when the track was downloaded, filled with black or a dark blur of the art. No amount of box-fitting could remove them, which is why the previous attempts did not. The cover is now scanned on load: the app walks in from each edge while the row or column stays flat and still matches the colour that edge started with, finds the real artwork inside, and shows only that region — scaled to fill, so nothing is padded and nothing else is cropped. It refuses to act on anything doubtful: padding on one side only means an off-centre picture rather than a frame, a trim deeper than 42% of a dimension is not padding, and an image it cannot read is shown whole. A little unevenness is tolerated, since a blurred backdrop is never perfectly flat. No frame around the Now-playing artwork, from any source. Two things could draw one and both are gone: `contain`, which pads whatever does not fit and leaves a hairline even when the ratio matches, and the coloured plate behind the image. That plate was a black one — but under a light wallpaper theme an earlier rule tinted the panel with a translucent wash, which is where the beige edge came from. The artwork now fills its box with `cover` on a transparent background, and the box takes the image's measured ratio, so in the ordinary case there is nothing to crop and nothing to pad. The ratio clamp is much wider (0.55–2.4), so square, 16:9, 5:4 and portrait covers are all shown whole; beyond it an extreme image loses a sliver rather than every normal one gaining a border. Covers keep their own shape, with no border around them. A square cover is shown square, a 16:9 cover is shown 16:9 — the box takes the image's measured ratio, and then uses cover rather than contain. Once the two agree those two show the same pixels, but contain could still leave a hairline of black from sub-pixel rounding, which is what the thin dark edges around 16:9 artwork were. The stylesheet's !important on that property had been silently beating the inline value. Bars now appear only when the ratio is clamped — an extreme banner or a tall poster — where showing the whole image matters more than avoiding them. Uniform grids are left alone on purpose: a results grid of ragged card heights is worse than a consistent crop. Sidebar playlists keep their name. The name was the row's only flexible item, so dragging the sidebar narrow made it absorb the whole shortfall and disappear, leaving a cover, a track count and two badges identifying nothing. Decoration gives way instead, in order: the count below 205px, the storage badge below 158px, the name never. New in Settings → Interface: Button labels — Adaptive drops the labels for icons once the track list goes narrow, or force Icons only / Always show labels; tooltips carry the meaning in every mode. Also there: a switch to hide playlist names in the sidebar on purpose, leaving the covers and counts. The follow-check button now uses the refresh arrow instead of a magnifier — a spinning magnifier meant nothing, and the arrow only spins while the check is actually running. The library header no longer runs off the right edge. Its button row had flex-shrink disabled, so the box sized itself to every button on one line and stayed that wide even after wrapping onto its own row — its own flex-wrap could never engage. The title block had no rule at all and kept a flex item's default minimum, so a long playlist name held the header open. The subtitle capped itself at 60vw, which measures the window rather than the column it sits in. Track columns now follow the list's measured width instead of the window's: collapsing the sidebar hands it ~270px and pinning the Now-playing drawer takes ~330px away, and neither changes the window size — so a wide window with the drawer docked used to squeeze Album into a few characters while a narrow window with the sidebar hidden had room and hid it anyway. Album drops below 560px of real width, the duration below 420px. The drawers now keep the same 8px gap on all four sides. They were anchored to the player's HEIGHT, but a height is a border box and excludes the player's own 8px bottom margin — so the offset landed exactly on the player's top edge and the panels sat flush against it: 8px at top, 8px at right, nothing at the bottom. The measurement is now the distance to the player's top edge, which folds the margin and the mobile safe-area inset in, and it updates on window resize as well as on the player's own size changes. Applies to Now playing, Downloads and the mobile sidebar alike. The Now-playing artwork no longer pads a video with black. The box was locked to a square while YouTube thumbnails are 16:9, so `contain` painted the difference as roughly 140px of dead black on a 320px-wide drawer, above and below the image. File album art is square and looked right, which is why the square held until a video played. The image is now measured and the box takes its real shape, clamped so an extreme asset cannot stretch the drawer into a strip. On windows under 560px the drawer takes the full width instead of leaving a strip of app too thin to read — at 405px it covered everything but a 64px sliver, which reads as a broken layout rather than an overlay. The top bar no longer jumps aside for a floating panel. Opening Now playing shrank the nav bar whether the panel was pinned or not, so the whole top row shifted on every open — for a bar that ends well before the panel's edge. Only the pinned panel, which is genuinely part of the layout, reserves space now. The storage badge is no longer eaten by long titles: title and badge shared one truncating box, so the ellipsis swallowed the pill exactly on the rows where knowing mattered. The title now ellipses on its own and the badge keeps its place, in the track list and in Up next. The Now-playing pin does what it says: pinned, the panel becomes a real column and the app shrinks around it; unpinned, it floats over the content. Window width used to decide that on its own, so the button seemed to do nothing and a wide window handed you a docked panel you never asked for. Now playing shows the storage badge on its title, and its "local file / streaming" line no longer lies about a downloaded YouTube track — the path still starts with yt: while the audio comes off the disk. The badge is sized in em, so it scales with whatever text it sits next to and stops nudging the rest of the row. The Now-playing and Downloads drawers now anchor to the player’s real height instead of a hard-coded offset that only ever matched one layout. Playlist cards in search results answer to right-click, like everything else in that view. Icons everywhere, and a single colour language for storage state. Blue cloud = streamed, needs the network. Green drive = came from YouTube but saved locally, plays offline. Red struck-through cloud = unavailable at the source. Plain local files carry no badge — tagging 1600 rows would turn the signal into wallpaper. The badge now appears on track rows, on the now-playing title, and as a per-playlist summary in the sidebar. Every button in the app has an icon. These three colours sit outside the usual purple accent on purpose: they answer a different question and must not read as selection. Everything the app says is in English again — the last batch had slipped into French. Behaviour is unchanged. Fixed: importing a playlist without "Save locally" no longer empties it. Tracks with no local file were all being hidden, but those stream perfectly well — only tracks the source refuses outright are hidden now, the ones that can neither be downloaded nor streamed. New Stats tab: most and least played tracks, top and least played artists, top albums, total plays and time listened. It required building a play counter first — the history deduplicates by track, so it only ever knew when you last played something, never how many times. Counting therefore starts from zero; past history does not hold this information. A play counts after 30s actually heard (half the duration for short tracks), read from the playback clock so pauses are excluded — flicking through with Next no longer inflates anything. Tracks never played are counted separately from least played. Import dialog: the playlist search is gone — it opens straight on the URL field. Downloads panel: yt-dlp's wall of text is reduced to a short label — a Premium-only video now reads 'Premium only' instead of the id, the repetition and a truncated sentence; the raw message stays in the tooltip. The Activity dot always shows and carries the batch state (purple running, red failed, amber canceled, green all through), and only pulses while something is actually running. The list is split into In progress / Waiting / Failed / Canceled / Saved, failures first. Ctrl+Enter searches in the background: the view stays put, the result parks in Activity and opens on click, and several can run at once without cancelling or overwriting each other. Follow checks appear in Activity with per-playlist progress instead of running invisibly. — Previous fixes still included: removing duplicates now actually saves. The playlist branch called PL._persist, which playlists.js does not export — optional chaining swallowed the call, so the cleanup lived in memory only and duplicates came back on restart. Scrolling no longer stutters: cover art was being re-scanned across every mounted row on each re-slice; it is now deferred and coalesced off the scroll path. Download counts only count what will actually be attempted — already-local and known-unavailable tracks are excluded and reported separately. After a batch, tracks the source refuses for good can be removed on confirmation. Newly downloaded tracks reappear immediately instead of staying hidden until the next restart. Online tracks now carry an icon instead of a text badge, with a distinct colour for unavailable ones. Adding by URL offers to download right away. Playlist Refresh re-fetches titles from the source instead of only rereading the local cache, and a followed playlist can be checked for new tracks on its own.
